questions.question: Define pollination and distinguish between self-pollination and cross-pollination, giving one advantage of each.
questions.expected_answer: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma of the same species. Self-pollination is transfer to the stigma of the same flower or another flower on the same plant; advantage: reliable, does not need an outside agent. Cross-pollination is transfer to a flower on a different plant of the same species; advantage: offspring are more varied, which helps the species survive disease and change.

questions.question: Compare the features of wind-pollinated and insect-pollinated flowers under the headings petals, nectar and scent, anthers and stigmas, and pollen.
questions.expected_answer: Petals: wind, small, dull or absent; insect, large and brightly coloured, often with nectar guides. Nectar and scent: wind, none; insect, nectar and usually scent. Anthers and stigmas: wind, anthers hang outside on long filaments, stigmas large and feathery outside the flower; insect, anthers and stigma inside the flower where visitors brush them. Pollen: wind, small, light, smooth, dry and produced in huge amounts; insect, larger, sticky or spiky, in smaller amounts.

questions.question: Explain why pollinators are important for food production in South Africa and suggest two ways to protect them.
questions.expected_answer: About a third of the food we eat comes from crops that need animal pollinators, mainly bees, including apples, pears, macadamias, avocados, citrus, pumpkins, sunflowers and canola; without them yields would drop and food would be scarcer, less varied and more expensive. Fruit farmers rent hives each spring. Protection: plant indigenous flowering plants and leave wild vegetation on farms; use pesticides carefully and not while bees are foraging; support beekeepers and control bee diseases.
